title: The hem of his cloak (Mark 5:25–34)
hookLine: twelve years bleeding, she reaches through the crowd and Jesus stops to find her

lines: A CROWD ON AN URGENT ERRAND.
cards: A crowd, pushing and shoving down a narrow street. Jesus is on an urgent errand: a synagogue leader's daughter is dying, and you'll hear about her tomorrow. Everyone presses close.
And somewhere in that crush is a woman nobody is looking at. For twelve years she's been bleeding.

Mark says she had suffered many things from many physicians, spent everything she had, and was no better, but rather worse. Twelve years of appointments, of hope, of bills. She doesn't ask for anything.
She doesn't want to be seen. She has one plan, and it's very small.

teach.h: IF I TOUCH BUT HIS GARMENT.
teach.b: Her plan, in the Douay-Rheims: "If I shall touch but his garment, I shall be whole." She comes up behind him in the crowd and touches his clothes.
Matthew and Luke say the hem, the fringe; some readers take that as one of the tassels the Law of Moses asks for at the corners of a garment.
At once, Mark says, the bleeding stops, and she feels in her body that she is healed.
She could slip away now. Nobody would know.

But Jesus stops, turns around in the crowd, and asks: "Who hath touched my garments?" His disciples are baffled: look at this crowd pressing on you, and you ask who touched you? He keeps looking around to see who did it.

There's a difference between being bumped and being reached for, and he felt the reach. The woman, afraid and trembling, comes forward, falls down before him, and tells him the whole truth, in front of everyone.
Why did he stop? Not to take the healing back. He wanted to meet her.
Leviticus counts a flow of blood like hers as ritual impurity, a matter of the Temple, not of sin. Mark doesn't say how her neighbors treated her; he says she'd lost her money and her health.
Now, in front of the whole crowd, Jesus calls her by a family word: "Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole: go in peace."

teach.h: DAUGHTER, THY FAITH HATH MADE THEE WHOLE.
teach.b: Healed in body, then named as family. An old tradition gives her a name, but the Gospels don't.

how: Catholics hear this Gospel at Sunday Mass together with the raising of Jairus's daughter, and some bring long illnesses to prayer and to the anointing of the sick.

games.q: you've touched his cloak and you feel healed. he stops and asks, who touched me? what do you do?
o: come forward, trembling, and tell him the whole truth.
point at someone else in the crush.
games.why: she comes forward, falls before him and tells the whole truth. he calls her daughter and sends her in peace.

practice: Think of help you've needed for a long time and haven't asked for: a doctor's appointment you keep postponing, a friend you haven't told, a counselor, a priest, a parent.
Maybe you've hoped to get it without anyone seeing; just name it, and imagine reaching out a little, the way she reached for the hem. If you pray, you can reach for God with it.

wordCard.voice: tassel. The fringe on Jesus's cloak that a suffering woman reached for in a crowd, and was healed.

orig.note: Greek: the edge or tassel of a garment. Matthew and Luke's word for what she touched.

carryVoice: Your line: he stopped for her. And in front of everyone, he called her daughter. Day forty, done.
